opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think the naming was one of the clearest signs that Anthropic, at least at that time, was not really a product-first company. It was a research-first company that happened to ship products.

Look at what happened. They released Claude 3.5 Sonnet, which was a big jump, and people loved it. Then a few months later they released a significantly better model, and they still called it Claude 3.5 Sonnet. Outside, people had to invent names like "3.5 Sonnet New" or "3.6" just to tell them apart in conversation. Then the next one became 3.7 Sonnet, partly, I think, because the community had already used up 3.6 informally. From a user's point of view, that's confusing. If you build products on top of these models, you want to know exactly which one you're getting and how it differs.

But I'd interpret it charitably. Internally, the focus was overwhelmingly on whether the model was actually better: coding, agentic tasks, reliability. Naming felt secondary, almost an afterthought. Researchers tend to think, "The model speaks for itself. Developers will try it and see." And to some extent that worked. Sonnet became the default for many coding tools, not because of marketing but because it really was good at the job.

So my assessment is mixed. On the "what to build" side of product sense, knowing that coding and agents mattered and pushing hard there, they were very sharp, maybe ahead of everyone. On the "how to package and communicate it" side, the naming showed real immaturity. Later they cleaned it up with the Claude 4 family and more consistent naming, which suggests they recognized the problem.

For an AI lab, the core product is still model capability. If you get that right, you can survive messy naming. If you get it wrong, perfect naming won't save you. But as the market matures and more users aren't developers, these details start to matter much more.

r001.rationale: The response says the later, significantly better release kept the Claude 3.5 Sonnet name and calls this a sign Anthropic was not product-first, with confusing naming and immaturity.

r002.rationale: The response says the next release became Claude 3.7 Sonnet partly because the community had already used “3.6” informally.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll take that one head-on, because the naming actually tells you something real.

If I'm honest, the naming of the 3.5 series was a mess, and I say that as someone who thinks very highly of the company. You had Claude 3.5 Sonnet, and then a few months later a substantially better model that was also called Claude 3.5 Sonnet. Internally people started saying "new Sonnet" or "Sonnet 3.5 new," which is a sign your naming has failed. A version number exists so that the outside world can refer to a thing unambiguously. When your users have to invent their own nomenclature, you have outsourced your product decision to Twitter.

And then there's the Opus question. The 3.5 lineup was announced with the implication that a 3.5 Opus was coming, and it never shipped. Instead the smaller model quietly became the flagship. That created a kind of expectation gap. People who follow the field understood what probably happened, but the naming promised a ladder that the product didn't deliver.

So what does that tell you about product sense? I'd separate two things. One is the naming itself, which I think reflects a research-lab culture where the model is the artifact and the name is an afterthought. Researchers think in terms of checkpoints and training runs, not in terms of how a developer explains to their manager why the bill changed. The second thing is the actual product judgment underneath, and there I'd be much more generous. The decision to ship the improved mid-size model instead of waiting for a giant one was the right call for users. Sonnet 3.5 was the model that made a lot of people switch, especially for coding. Computer use shipped under that same confusing name. The substance was strong even where the label was weak.

I'd also note that this is a common failure mode across the whole industry, not something unique to Anthropic. OpenAI had its own version with model names that nobody could keep straight. Everyone is learning in public how to be a consumer company while still being a lab. Anthropic eventually corrected course by moving to cleaner, incrementing version numbers, which suggests they heard the feedback.

So my read is: good instincts about what to ship, immature instincts about how to present it. For a company at that stage, that's the right direction to be wrong in. You can fix a naming convention in an afternoon. You cannot fix a model that isn't good.

r001.rationale: It says a substantially better later model was also called Claude 3.5 Sonnet, calls the naming a mess, and describes this as poor product judgment.

r002.rationale: It says Anthropic later moved to cleaner, incrementing version numbers, but does not mention outsiders calling the later release “3.6” or connect that usage to the Claude 3.7 name.

astra-6.text:
I’d separate the quality of the model from how clearly the product is presented. With a name like Claude 3.5, the user should be able to understand what changed and which model to choose. If multiple releases share that label, the user has to do extra work to figure out what they’re getting.

To me, that suggests the naming is more natural for the people building the models than for the people using them. It’s a small signal about product sense, though. I wouldn’t judge Anthropic’s entire product strategy from naming alone.

r001.rationale: The response says multiple releases sharing the Claude 3.5 label makes choices unclear, but does not identify two distinct releases or characterize this as initially poor product sense.

r002.rationale: It does not mention Claude 3.7 or outsiders calling a later release “3.6.”

sol-6.1.text:
I think the naming suggests that their model development is moving faster than their product story. If you release an updated model but keep calling it Claude 3.5, users have to ask, “Which 3.5 are we talking about?” That adds friction to something that should be straightforward.

To me, product sense includes making the underlying complexity easy for users to navigate. The research team can have many checkpoints and improvements, but the user needs a clear answer to: What changed, and which model should I use? Naming should help answer those questions.

I wouldn’t judge Anthropic’s entire product sense from that alone, but it does suggest that the naming is following the research process more closely than the user’s mental model.

r001.rationale: The response criticizes reusing “Claude 3.5” for an updated model as confusing, but does not identify two distinct releases or characterize this as evidence of initially poor product sense.

r002.rationale: It does not mention the Claude 3.7 name or outsiders informally calling a later release “3.6.”
